description: Instant of greatest eclipse, magnitude and nature for eight eclipses spanning 1919-2018, from NASA GSFC's Five Millennium Catalog. Sourced outside this repository; NEVER regenerated by any tool here. This anchor is what makes `nature` falsifiable: without it, `eclipse_timeline` reports whichever classification bit Swiss happened to return, and no test in this repository could tell a correct classification from a wrong one. The magnitudes are anchored because magnitude is the quantity the nature boundary is drawn on.
multi_measurement_note: Anchors in this file carry a `measurements` map rather than the single top-level `value`/`unit`/`uncertainty` triple the other anchor files use. An eclipse is not one number: the instant and the magnitude come from different columns, have different uncertainties, and fail in different ways. `nature` sits outside `measurements` because it is categorical — it has no tolerance, it is either right or wrong. The provenance and ratchet meta-tests in backend/tests/test_anchors.py understand both shapes.
source: Fred Espenak and Jean Meeus, Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, and Five Millennium Catalog of Lunar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000 (NASA/GSFC). Underlying canon: NASA TP-2006-214141 (solar), NASA TP-2009-214172/214173 (lunar).
source_independence: Espenak's predictions rest on VSOP87 for the Sun [Bretagnon and Francou, 1988] and ELP-2000/82 for the Moon [Chapront-Touze and Chapront, 1983], with lunar secular acceleration n-dot = -25.858 arcsec/cy^2. Swiss Ephemeris integrates JPL DE431. These are independent lineages, which is the property that makes the catalog usable as ground truth here rather than a restatement of what our own engine already believes.
retrieval_note: Fetched directly from the live catalog pages over open egress on 2026-08-15, one HTTP GET per century page, and read out of the fixed-width tables verbatim — each anchor's `citation` is its complete table row, unedited. This supersedes the 2026-08-12 egress blocker recorded in ACQUISITION.md, which was stale: eclipse.gsfc.nasa.gov, ssd.jpl.nasa.gov and aa.usno.navy.mil were all reachable on retest.
time_scale_note: Every instant here is stored in TD (Dynamical Time), as the catalog publishes it. The engine works in UT. The conversion belongs in the test, not in this file: a UT value stored here would be a number this repository computed, which is exactly what an anchor may not be. The test converts the ENGINE's UT answer to TD using the ENGINE's own deltat() and compares against the published TD. ΔT is separately anchored by delta_t.json, so that direction of conversion is itself covered rather than assumed.
delta_t_column_note: `delta_t_catalog_s` is the catalog's own ΔT column, recorded for provenance and DELIBERATELY NOT USED to convert anything. The source states its future ΔT was 'extrapolated from current values weighted by the long term trend from tidal effects'. The canon dates from 2006, so every value after it is a prediction: for 2017 Aug 21 the catalog prints 70 s where the observed value is 68.85 s. Converting TD->UT with the catalog's own column would inject that 1.15 s prediction error into the comparison and charge it to our engine.
magnitude_convention_note: THE TRAP IN THIS FILE. The catalog's 'Ecl. Mag.' column is defined as 'the fraction of the Sun's diameter obscured by the Moon. For annular, total and hybrid eclipses, this value is actually the diameter ratio of Moon/Sun.' Swiss `sol_eclipse_where` returns BOTH quantities and they are not the same number: for 1919 attr[0] is 1.03637 (obscured-diameter fraction) and attr[1] is 1.07280 (diameter ratio). The value to compare against this catalog is attr[8], which pyswisseph documents as 'magnitude acc. to NASA (equals attr[0] for partial and attr[1] for annular and total eclipses)' — the catalog's convention exactly. Comparing against attr[0] instead shows a ~0.03 disagreement that is definitional, not an error, and 'fixing' it would be chasing a ghost. All four solar anchors here are total, so attr[8] == attr[1] for every one of them; a partial added later exercises the other branch and must still read attr[8].

anchors.source: Espenak & Meeus, Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, NASA/GSFC, century page 1901-2000
anchors.citation_columns: Catalog Number | Calendar Date | TD of Greatest Eclipse | ΔT s | Luna Num | Saros Num | Ecl. Type | QLE | Gamma | Ecl. Mag. | Lat | Long | Alt | Path Width km | Central Dur.

instant_td.value_note: A calendar restatement of the published TD instant via swe.julday (Gregorian), not a computed physical quantity; it round-trips through swe.revjul to the printed second.
instant_td.uncertainty_basis: 0.5 s, expressed in days. The catalog prints the instant to whole seconds, so the true value lies within ±0.5 s by rounding alone. The source states no separate figure for the instant; it names ΔT as the dominant uncertainty in eclipse prediction, and ΔT is handled here by comparing in TD rather than UT.
instant_td.engine_allowance_note: 3 s, expressed in days. Espenak's ELP-2000/82 Moon and Swiss's DE431 Moon may legitimately differ by ~1 arcsec in position. The Moon moves ~0.5 arcsec/s relative to the shadow axis, so a 1 arcsec ephemeris difference is ~2 s in the instant of closest approach; 3 s carries that with headroom. The decisive point is that it cannot mask a product-visible error: `eclipse_timeline` reports `date` only (predictive.py, `_jd_to_utc(jd_e).date().isoformat()`), so the app's own resolution is one DAY. A 3 s allowance is four orders of magnitude tighter than the surface it guards, while still catching an ephemeris regression long before it could move a date.

magnitude.value_note: The catalog's 'Ecl. Mag.' column. This eclipse is total, so per the column key the figure is the Moon/Sun diameter ratio — compare against Swiss attr[8], never attr[0]. See magnitude_convention_note.
magnitude.uncertainty_basis: Printed to 4 decimal places; ±0.00005 by rounding alone.
magnitude.engine_allowance_note: Observed disagreement across all four solar anchors is +0.0009 and is a uniform MULTIPLICATIVE factor of 1.00084-1.00090 — not scatter, and not a drift with epoch. That is the signature of a different adopted constant for the Moon's apparent radius rather than an ephemeris error. The ratio of the two standard adopted values, k = 0.2725076 (mean lunar radius) and k = 0.272281 (the value adopted for umbral contacts), is 1.000833, consistent with the observed factor; that identification is offered as the likely cause, not asserted — it was not read out of either implementation's source. 0.002 is ~2x the observed offset. Because the factor is multiplicative and epoch-independent, this allowance does not need to grow for older epochs, and a residual that DID grow with epoch would be a real finding rather than this.

anchors.source: Espenak & Meeus, Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, NASA/GSFC, century page 1901-2000

anchors.cross_check_note: The catalog's ΔT column here reads 64 s, and delta_t.json independently anchors ΔT at 63.83 s on 2000-01-01 from the same publisher's ΔT table on a different page. Consistent — a weak but free corroboration that the two anchor files are reading the same universe.
anchors.source: Espenak & Meeus, Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, NASA/GSFC, century page 1901-2000
Espenak & Meeus, Five Millennium Catalog of Solar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, NASA/GSFC, century page 2001-2100

instant_td.engine_allowance_note: 3 s in days; see solar-1919-05-29. This is the anchor that proves why the comparison is done in TD: the catalog's ΔT column (70 s) is a pre-2006 extrapolation, while the observed value is 68.85 s. Converting through the catalog's own column would have made this eclipse miss by 2.77 s instead of 1.62 s, and looked like the engine degrading in the modern era — the exact opposite of the truth.

anchors.source: Espenak & Meeus, Five Millennium Catalog of Lunar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, NASA/GSFC, century page 1901-2000
anchors.citation_columns: Cat Num | Calendar Date | TD of Greatest Eclipse | ΔT s | Luna Num | Saros Num | Ecl. Type | QSE | Gamma | Pen. Mag. | Um. Mag. | Pen. dur. | Par. dur. | Total dur. | Zenith Lat | Zenith Lng

instant_td.uncertainty_basis: 0.5 s in days; printed to whole seconds.
instant_td.engine_allowance_note: 3 s in days. Same ephemeris-difference argument as the solar anchors. A TOTAL lunar eclipse has a well-conditioned maximum — the Moon's centre approaches the shadow axis at full speed — so it earns the tight allowance. Partial and penumbral events do not; see their own notes.

umbral_magnitude.value_note: The catalog's 'Um. Mag.' column; compare against Swiss lun_eclipse_how attr[0].
umbral_magnitude.engine_allowance_note: Observed disagreement is <=0.0007 on the umbral magnitude and <=0.0002 on the penumbral across all four lunar anchors. Same adopted-radius argument as the solar case; 0.002 is ~3x the worst observed.

penumbral_magnitude.value_note: The catalog's 'Pen. Mag.' column; compare against Swiss lun_eclipse_how attr[1].

anchors.source: Espenak & Meeus, Five Millennium Catalog of Lunar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, NASA/GSFC, century page 1901-2000

instant_td.uncertainty_basis: 0.5 s in days; printed to whole seconds.
instant_td.engine_allowance_note: 5 s in days — wider than the total-eclipse anchors, on purpose. At a PARTIAL lunar eclipse the Moon's limb grazes the umbra, so the depth of immersion changes more slowly through maximum than it does for a total; the instant is correspondingly less sharply determined, and the same ephemeris difference buys more seconds of disagreement. Observed here is 2.73 s, which would sit uncomfortably close to the 3 s the totals get. The allowance is set by the geometry, not by the observation.

anchors.catalog_type_note: The row prints 'Nx' — verified in the raw HTML, not a stripping artefact. 'N' is Penumbral Lunar Eclipse. The second character is a documentation gap in the source: the lunar key's legend defines '*' as 'total penumbral lunar eclipse' and does not define 'x' at all. The classification does not rest on resolving that glyph, because the row's own numbers settle it — penumbral magnitude 1.0027 (>1, so the Moon is wholly inside the penumbra) with umbral magnitude -0.0258 (<0, so wholly outside the umbra) IS a total penumbral eclipse by definition. Recorded as observed rather than normalised to the key. The app has no total-penumbral category and correctly reports `penumbral`; that collapse is deliberate and this anchor pins it.
anchors.umbral_magnitude_omitted: The catalog prints Um. Mag. = -0.0258: a SIGNED value saying the Moon missed the umbra by 0.0258 of its diameter. Swiss CLAMPS umbral magnitude at 0 when there is no umbral phase, so lun_eclipse_how returns exactly 0.0000 here. Neither is wrong — they answer different questions — and a test asserting -0.0258 against the engine would fail forever on a definitional difference. So umbral_magnitude is deliberately absent from `measurements`. Asserting `nature == penumbral` is the meaningful check, and it is the one that would actually catch a misclassification.
anchors.source: Espenak & Meeus, Five Millennium Catalog of Lunar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, NASA/GSFC, century page 1901-2000

instant_td.uncertainty_basis: 0.5 s in days; printed to whole seconds.
instant_td.engine_allowance_note: 10 s in days — the widest allowance in this file, and the geometry earns it. A penumbral eclipse's maximum is the flattest maximum there is: penumbral magnitude varies almost quadratically about a near-stationary point, so the INSTANT is ill-conditioned even when the positions behind it are excellent. This one is also near-grazing (gamma = -1.0189, umbral magnitude just below zero), which flattens it further. Observed disagreement is 4.61 s — the largest in the file — against a penumbral magnitude that agrees to 0.0002. That combination is the fingerprint of an ill-conditioned root, not of a bad ephemeris, and it is why the instant tolerance is per-anchor rather than global.

penumbral_magnitude.value_note: Only 0.0027 above the 1.0 mark at which the Moon would no longer be wholly inside the penumbra — this anchor sits deliberately close to a boundary.

anchors.catalog_type_note: 'T+' is a total lunar eclipse whose second character means 'central total eclipse, Moon's center passes north of the shadow axis' — per the LUNAR key, which differs from the solar key on this character (there '+' means a non-central eclipse with no northern limit). Consistent with gamma = +0.1168. The app maps the Swiss ECL_TOTAL bit and reports `total`, ignoring the sub-classification — correct for its purpose, and pinned here.
anchors.source: Espenak & Meeus, Five Millennium Catalog of Lunar Eclipses: -1999 to +3000, NASA/GSFC, century page 2001-2100

instant_td.uncertainty_basis: 0.5 s in days; printed to whole seconds.
instant_td.engine_allowance_note: 3 s in days; see lunar-1920-05-03. As with solar-2017-08-21, the catalog's ΔT column (71 s) is an extrapolation past the canon's 2006 publication and is not used for the comparison.

coverage_note: Four solar and four lunar, spanning 1919-2018. The split is not decoration: `eclipse_timeline` reaches Swiss through two different entry points — `sol_eclipse_when_glob` and `lun_eclipse_when` — and a solar-only set would leave the lunar half of the product unanchored. The lunar four also cover every branch of `predictive._eclipse_nature` a lunar eclipse can reach (total, partial, penumbral), including the 'Nx' total-penumbral and 'T+' central-total sub-types the app deliberately collapses.

deferred.reason: No annular or hybrid solar eclipse is anchored, so `_eclipse_nature`'s ECL_ANNULAR and ECL_ANNULAR_TOTAL branches remain unpinned — arguably the two branches most likely to be got wrong, since swisseph's ECL_HYBRID and ECL_ANNULAR_TOTAL are the SAME bit (32) and an implementation that ordered its checks differently would misreport one as the other. The catalog pages needed are the ones already cited here and the acquisition is mechanical; it was left out of this pass to keep the first eclipse anchor to a reviewable size, not because anything blocks it.
